title: From orthonormal bases to least squares
learningObjective: Explain least-squares solutions through orthogonal projection onto a column space.

retrieve.bodyMarkdown: A closest-point residual is orthogonal to the entire target subspace. How can a basis reduce that condition to finitely many equations?

encounter.bodyMarkdown: Three measurements may not fit a model exactly. The best fit is not an arbitrary compromise: its residual is perpendicular to every direction the model can produce.

explain.bodyMarkdown: Gram–Schmidt builds an orthonormal basis from an independent list: subtract projections onto earlier unit vectors, then normalize the nonzero residual. For orthonormal columns $q_i$, projection is $\sum_i\langle b,q_i\rangle q_i$. For a real matrix $A$, the vectors $Ax$ fill its column space. Minimizing $\|Ax-b\|^2$ is therefore projection, characterized by $A^T(Ax-b)=0$, the normal equations. If the columns are independent, $A^TA$ is invertible because $x^TA^TAx=\|Ax\|^2>0$ for nonzero $x$. If columns are dependent, the closest output is still unique but its coefficients need not be.

reflect.bodyMarkdown: Distinguish the fitted vector from the parameter vector. Orthogonal projection is unique even when redundant model columns produce several coefficient lists.

problems.promptMarkdown: In Gram–Schmidt, what follows subtracting the projections onto earlier orthonormal vectors?

hints.bodyMarkdown: Separate removal of old directions from setting the length.
An orthonormal vector must be orthogonal and have unit norm.
Subtracting projections achieves only the first condition.
The residual is orthogonal to the earlier vectors. For independent input vectors it is nonzero, so divide by its norm to obtain a unit vector.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The residual is orthogonal to the earlier vectors. For independent input vectors it is nonzero, so divide by its norm to obtain a unit vector.

problems.promptMarkdown: For $u=(1,0)$ and $v=(1,2)$, subtract the projection of $v$ onto $u$. What is the norm of the residual?

hints.bodyMarkdown: Find the residual before measuring its length.
Project onto the first coordinate axis.
Only the second coordinate remains.
The projection is $(1,0)$, leaving $(0,2)$ of norm two. Normalizing would yield $(0,1)$.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The projection is $(1,0)$, leaving $(0,2)$ of norm two. Normalizing would yield $(0,1)$.

problems.promptMarkdown: Which equation characterizes a least-squares solution to $Ax\approx b$?

hints.bodyMarkdown: Express orthogonality to every model direction.
Columns span the possible outputs.
Multiplication by the transpose collects dot products with columns.
The residual must be orthogonal to every column of $A$. Stacking these dot products yields $A^T(Ax-b)=0$.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The residual must be orthogonal to every column of $A$. Stacking these dot products yields $A^T(Ax-b)=0$.

problems.promptMarkdown: Fit a constant $c$ to measurements $2,4,9$ by minimizing $(c-2)^2+(c-4)^2+(c-9)^2$. Find $c$.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Treat the constant model as a one-column linear map.
Apply the normal equation or require the residual sum to vanish.
The three measurements sum to fifteen.
The column is $(1,1,1)$, so the normal equation is $3c=2+4+9=15$. Thus $c=5$, the mean.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The column is $(1,1,1)$, so the normal equation is $3c=2+4+9=15$. Thus $c=5$, the mean.

problems.promptMarkdown: Prove that independent columns make $A^TA$ invertible.

steps.textMarkdown: Assume $A$ has independent columns and let $A^TAx=0$.
Multiply on the left by $x^T$ to obtain $\|Ax\|^2=0$.
The square matrix $A^TA$ has zero kernel, so it is invertible.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Show the normal-equation matrix has zero kernel.
Connect its quadratic expression with a squared norm.
Independent columns make $Ax=0$ possible only for $x=0$.
A squared norm can vanish only at zero. Column independence then removes all nontrivial kernel vectors of the square matrix.

problems.solutionMarkdown: A squared norm can vanish only at zero. Column independence then removes all nontrivial kernel vectors of the square matrix.
